frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, use of Windows Credential Manager APIs, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of any credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or registry hives, and no anomalous credential-related events on the compromised Windows hosts.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: All process creations and file writes are standard Windows/Azure tooling; no dumping utilities, no hive copies, no dump files beyond WER crash dumps.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: LSASS opens with high access masks come from PowerShell/wsmprovhost .NET process-management calls (managed call traces) and from wininit/csrss during a normal lsass restart; no MiniDump/comsvcs/procdump activity.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: SAM registry writes and SAM_SERVER/SAM_DOMAIN handle opens are performed by lsass.exe (machine account) as normal OS SAM operations; no reg save or hive file copies.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntds.dit file access, no ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow command lines, no shadow-copy or NTDS activity in any dataset.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No LSA Secrets access; no process/script referencing secrets/lsadump, and no SECURITY Policy Secrets object access.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes are made by lsass.exe itself as normal cached-credential maintenance, not extraction.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No DCSync/drsuapi/lsadump activity in process command lines or PowerShell script blocks.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity is a 7-second netsh 'trace start capture=yes' / 'trace stop' pair on scranton.dmevals.local, both spawned by the signed Microsoft Azure NetworkWatcherAgent service (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service) — a legitimate Azure Network Watcher capture. No sniffing tools (tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap/dumpcap), no Npcap/WinPcap driver load, no pcap files, and no promiscuous-mode commands were observed. The credential-access activity in the window (PsExec with cleartext password, python C2 payload) is not network sniffing.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Steganographic PowerShell loader (monkey.png, hidden window, -ep bypass) on scranton.dmevals.local ran Invoke-Exfil with hardcoded credentials and WebDAV exfiltration, and its process opened LSASS with full access.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: No keylogger indicators (GetAsyncKeyState/SetWindowsHookEx/keylog strings) found in Sysmon command lines or PowerShell script blocks.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: No GUI credential prompt capture artifacts identified; observed credential activity is LSASS access and hardcoded-credential use.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No IIS/wwwroot/inetpub login-page or w3wp web-portal capture artifacts found; zeek window non-overlapping and showed no HTTP POST.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell PID 2976 on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_VM_READ/ALL_ACCESS), the access pattern for reading LSASS credential memory.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625 failed-logon events in windows.security; only successful 4648 explicit-credential logons from PsExec and system accounts.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No 4625 failures and no password-referencing command lines or script blocks; no guessing activity.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No cracking tooling, wordlists/potfiles, or SAM/SECURITY hive reads; lsass access is benign svchost 0x1000 queries.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No 4625 failures; 4648 logons are PsExec and normal system accounts, not a spray pattern.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No 4625 failures and no credential/password script blocks or command lines indicating credential stuffing.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smart-card/OTP interception artifacts in any dataset. Credential-related registry/service hits are standard Windows components (CredentialEnrollmentManager, Credential Manager vaultsvc, scfilter.sys smart card PnP driver, RDP display driver, CredentialGuard disabled). LSASS access is only benign svchost.exe PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION (0x1000) queries. The observed credential activity is PsExec lateral movement with cleartext credentials (T1078/T1021), not MFA interception.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: Confirmed forced authentication: on scranton.dmevals.local the WebClient service spawned rundll32.exe 'davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav' (5x, user pbeesly), and Zeek shows the matching WebDAV OPTIONS/PROPFIND traffic from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4 with Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/DavClnt user agents and 401 challenges. This is the classic T1187 WebDAV credential-coercion pattern, occurring alongside a broader compromise of the host.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: LSASS was opened with full-access masks (0x1FFFFF, 0x1F3FFF) by PowerShell.exe on scranton.dmevals.local and by wsmprovhost.exe (WinRM remote PowerShell) on nashua.dmevals.local, with call traces through PowerShell/.NET modules — consistent with in-memory credential dumping via exploitation/credential-access tooling. Kerberos and Zeek hits were benign.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: All T1539-relevant hits are benign: the only 'cookie' process activity is the Windows WebDAV client davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie (rundll32.exe, parent svchost.exe) on scranton; the only cookie-named file creation is the WARP JIT service's own INetCookies store under the LocalService profile; Edge process-access/file-write events come solely from legitimate Windows components (Explorer.EXE, svchost.exe, ctfmon.exe, browser_broker.exe) with standard access masks. No browser cookie store (Chrome/Edge/Firefox Cookies, Login Data, Web Data) was touched by any non-browser process, and no credential-stealer tooling (mimikatz/procdump/pypykatz/lsass dump/DPAPI/vault) was observed. No evidence of web session cookie theft.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Credential material collected to disk (passwordsDB, .pfx) and reused in cleartext for lateral movement.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Hardcoded cleartext credentials in PsExec64 command line (dmevals\pbeesly / Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by), accesschk writing 'passwordsDB', and password-protected RAR staging of working.zip on NASHUA.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All Password/Credential registry value sets are legitimate OS components (svchost, lsass, services, winlogon).

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No consolehost_history or shell-history file access found in sysmon/security telemetry.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys PowerShell function exported all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx files on scranton.dmevals.local, then staged/exfiltrated via 7z to a WebDAV share.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: GptTmpl.inf/gpt.ini sysvol reads are routine Group Policy processing by machine accounts; no Groups.xml cpassword access observed.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: Private-key .pfx export and passwordsDB file creation indicate credential-store harvesting on scranton.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: PowerShell wrote a private-key .pfx (coyn5igj.3io.pfx) to Downloads on scranton.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: Full-access LSASS handle requests (0x1fffff / 0x1f3fff) are consistent with harvesting DPAPI/Credential Manager secrets from LSASS memory, but no direct cmdkey/vaultcmd/Credential Manager registry or file artifacts were logged.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No password-manager executables, .kdbx files, or password-manager process access found in any dataset.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:05:16, consistent with credential dumping from the authentication process; the loader was a hidden-window -ep bypass PowerShell spawned from control.exe with a bitmap-steganography IEX payload.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: 4624 type-3 logons are machine-account (NEWYORK$/SCRANTON$) noise; 4648 explicit-credential logons reflect pbeesly credential reuse to NASHUA via PSEXESVC (lateral movement), not DC authentication modification.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No Notification Packages/PasswordFilter registry writes, no password-filter process creation, no password-filter script blocks; only legitimate Microsoft DLL loads (cryptdll/samlib/samcli).

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739 events, no Reversible/Set-ADUser/dsmod command lines, no AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption script blocks.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/5136 events and no Set-ADUser/Set-ADAccountControl process creation; no MFA configuration changes.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 events and no Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD script blocks; only legitimate AD module resource strings.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider/Credential Provider registry writes and no NetworkProvider/New-ItemProperty script blocks.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: Two MACs (00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) claim IP 10.0.1.4; the second appears only from 00:33:26 and exclusively targets 10.0.1.6 (NASHUA) on SMB/WinRM/RPC/HTTP, indicating on-path AiTM positioning.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: Spoofed 10.0.1.4 drives SMB 445/WinRM 5985/RPC 135 to NASHUA with Kerberos TGS for cifs/NASHUA and HTTP/NASHUA (pbeesly), consistent with SMB relay/name-resolution poisoning, but no explicit relay tooling or LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning was observed.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: A single IP (10.0.1.4) is claimed by a new MAC (fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) mid-capture while the legitimate MAC persists, the classic ARP cache poisoning / MAC takeover signature.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP events in any dataset: no DHCP codes in windows.other, no dhcp log type in Zeek, and no DHCP PowerShell script blocks.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) with an UNKNOWN-module CallTrace, and a reflective shellcode loader script block executed on the same host minutes later — credential/ticket theft from LSASS memory.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: Only normal krbtgt TGS requests (encryption type 0x12, status 0x0); no forged-ticket or RC4-downgrade indicators.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: Service-ticket requests are normal machine-account/krbtgt requests with matching TGTs; no silver-ticket behavior.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No Kerberoast tooling in PowerShell logs and no burst of TGS requests to many SPNs in the zeek kerberos capture.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: AS exchanges show KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED (preauth enforced) — normal flow, not AS-REP roasting; no AS-REP tooling found.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential artifacts. The credential-related activity present (PowerShell.exe opening lsass.exe with 0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF and an obfuscated base64-shellcode PowerShell script as pbeesly on scranton) is credential theft (T1003), not T1606 forging of web credentials.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only cookie-path file event is a benign Windows INetCookies package file created by svchost.exe; no browser cookie theft/tampering or forged-cookie authentication. Zeek HTTP is WebDAV file transfer only.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: No SAML/ADFS/token/assertion references in process command lines, PowerShell script blocks, or HTTP URLs. Zeek window has no federated/web auth traffic; only a single NtLmSsp network logon consistent with post-theft lateral movement.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA request generation artifacts: zero 4625 failed-logon events in windows.security (no repeated auth attempts), no MFA/2FA/Authenticator/multifactor strings in PowerShell 4104 script blocks, no mfa/authenticator/login in Sysmon process command lines, and no login/auth/mfa/okta/duo URLs or DNS queries in Zeek. The windows.other 5857/5858 hits are benign NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM RSOP/WMI DeleteInstance operations on newyork.dmevals.local. The only credential-related activity is PsExec lateral movement by pbeesly, which is not T1621.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: Certificate private-key export to .pfx (coyn5igj.3io.pfx) observed on scranton.

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot credential-dumping tools (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll rundll32) among rare executables.
Stack process-access targets to find LSASS or other credential-store processes being opened.
Stack object types accessed under handle/object-access auditing to find SAM/SECURITY/LSASS objects.
Stack newly created processes to spot dumping utilities launched on hosts.

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell script blocks referencing LSASS/credential-dumping APIs.
Look for credential-dumping references in other Windows event channels (service installs, VSS, etc.).

Read individual LSASS access events with source image and granted access.

findings.title: Steganographic PowerShell payload (monkey.png) executed with hidden window and bypass
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, control.exe spawned PowerShell (PID 2976) with '-noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden' that decodes a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png via System.Drawing pixel extraction and executes it with IEX. This hidden, execution-policy-bypassing loader is the process that subsequently accessed LSASS with full access, consistent with an input/credential capture toolchain.

findings.title: Invoke-Exfil PowerShell script with hardcoded credentials and WebDAV exfiltration

This is credential-handling and exfiltration activity by the same user whose PowerShell accessed LSASS.

findings.title: PowerShell process opened LSASS with full access rights (credential API access)
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, a PowerShell process (PID 2976, launched by control.exe with a steganographic monkey.png payload) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z. These masks include PROCESS_VM_READ and PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, the access pattern used to read LSASS memory for credential extraction (API access to credential material). The same process ran the Invoke-Exfil script, indicating an active credential-access/exfiltration toolchain.

findings.title: WebDAV forced authentication via davclnt DavSetCookie on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On host scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly, the WebClient service (svchost.exe -k LocalService -p -s WebClient) spawned rundll32.exe executing 'C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav' five times between 03:08:50 and 03:10:23 UTC on 2020-05-02. This is the canonical T1187 forced-authentication mechanism: the WebClient/WebDAV redirector is pointed at an attacker-controlled host (192.168.0.4) so the victim's machine authenticates to it, leaking NTLM credentials. The matching network side (Zeek, 2020-04-30 window) shows the same host 10.0.1.4 issuing WebDAV OPTIONS/PROPFIND requests to 192.168.0.4 with user agents 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362' and 'DavClnt', including PROPFIND for /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z and /webdav/python.exe, with repeated 401 Unauthorized responses (the server challenging for credentials). This activity occurs in the context of a broader compromise of scranton (malicious C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr launched by explorer.exe, PowerShell stager, sdelete64 anti-forensics), consistent with an adversary harvesting credentials.

findings.title: LSASS memory accessed with full-access rights by PowerShell and WinRM host processes
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local a PowerShell.exe process (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1F3FFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, with a call trace through ntdll/KERNELBASE and an UNKNOWN module — the classic signature of in-memory credential dumping (e.g. Mimikatz-style LSASS read). On nashua.dmevals.local a wsmprovhost.exe process (PID 7720, the WinRM remote-PowerShell host) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 2020-05-02T03:09:29Z, its call trace running through .NET/PowerShell native images (System.ni.dll, Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll), i.e. credential access driven from a remote PowerShell session. Both events run as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. These are the only non-system processes in the dataset touching lsass with such broad access masks; the remaining 289 lsass accesses are from svchost.exe with 0x1000 (query-limited) and are benign.

On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell (user pbeesly) repeatedly launched C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\PsExec64.exe with the cleartext credential pair -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by to remotely execute C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on \\NASHUA (4 starts between 03:11 and 03:14). This is credential material embedded in a command line, consistent with unsecured-credentials usage and lateral movement using harvested credentials.

PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx files
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script (Path: C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) defining function Get-PrivateKeys. findings.title: Interactive PowerShell credential-dumping session by pbeesly accessing LSASS memory on scranton and nashua
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 the account pbeesly ran an interactive PowerShell attack session on scranton.dmevals.local (keystroke logging, screen capture, clipboard theft, Invoke-Exfil) and opened handles to lsass.exe with full-access masks. On scranton, powershell.exe requested a handle to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, including 'Read from process memory'), and Sysmon recorded powershell.exe accessing lsass.exe. Using Invoke-Command -ComputerName NASHUA, the same user's remote session on nashua.dmevals.local (wsmprovhost.exe) requested lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1f3fff. Reading LSASS memory is the standard way to harvest credentials from Windows password stores (DPAPI/Credential Manager secrets).

LSASS handle requests with full-access masks consistent with harvesting Windows Credential Manager/DPAPI secrets
findings.summary: The same pbeesly activity that targeted LSASS used access masks (0x1fffff on scranton via powershell.exe, 0x1f3fff on nashua via wsmprovhost.exe) that include 'Read from process memory' and 'Duplicate handle into or out of process' — the rights needed to extract DPAPI master keys and Credential Manager vault secrets held in LSASS. No cmdkey/vaultcmd command lines, no Credential Manager registry/file artifacts (Sysmon 15 on *Credentials*, 4688 with vault/cmdkey) were observed, so the Credential Manager-specific store access is inferred from the LSASS memory access rather than directly logged.

On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, launched from control.exe with -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden and a bitmap-steganography IEX payload) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff — PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, the classic credential-dumping access mask. This is credential theft from the authentication process rather than modification of it: no registry writes to LSA/Notification Packages/NetworkProvider, no password-filter DLL, no reversible-encryption or MFA changes were observed. The stolen credentials were then used in cleartext by PsExec64 to reach NASHUA.
findings.title: LSASS memory accessed with full access rights by PowerShell on scranton (credential theft, not authentication-process modification)
Adversary-in-the-Middle positioning via ARP poisoning on the 10.0.1.0/24 segment
findings.summary: The overarching AiTM activity is the MAC takeover of 10.0.1.4 by fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 from 00:33:26, redirecting 10.0.1.4<->10.0.1.6 (NASHUA) SMB/WinRM/RPC/HTTP flows through the attacker. The legitimate MAC 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 continues to be seen for the same IP, confirming two devices claiming one address. This is the on-path positioning that enables the credential access observed in the Kerberos cifs/NASHUA and HTTP/NASHUA ticket requests.

findings.title: ARP cache poisoning: MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 impersonates IP 10.0.1.4 to intercept traffic to NASHUA (10.0.1.6)
findings.summary: In the Zeek capture (2020-04-30 00:06-00:45) host IP 10.0.1.4 is seen with two different source MAC addresses. The legitimate MAC 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 is present across the whole window (134 connections, 00:06:38-00:45:00), while a second MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 appears only from 00:33:26 onward (44 connections) and exclusively targets 10.0.1.6 (NASHUA) on SMB/445, WinRM/5985, RPC/135 and HTTP/80. A single IP being claimed by a new MAC mid-capture is the signature of ARP cache poisoning / MAC takeover, positioning the attacker in the middle of 10.0.1.4<->10.0.1.6 traffic. Kerberos TGS requests for pbeesly/DMEVALS.LOCAL to cifs/NASHUA and HTTP/NASHUA follow immediately, consistent with credential use against the victim.

findings.title: PowerShell opens LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (0x1fffff) on scranton — credential/ticket theft staging
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.654Z, with a CallTrace ending in an UNKNOWN module (UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D)) — the classic signature of in-memory credential/ticket extraction. This is the only non-system process among the LSASS handle-grant events with full access; the other 0x1fffff grants come from legitimate system processes (wininit.exe, csrss.exe). Minutes later, at 2020-05-02T03:21:29Z on the same host, a PowerShell script block (ScriptBlockId bc19aae2-d1f9-49b2-b718-192531ae928f, user pbeesly) executed a reflective shellcode loader using GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle via Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods and a base64-encoded PE payload. Together these indicate an adversary on scranton stealing credentials/tickets from LSASS memory.

findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates with private keys to .pfx on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly, a PowerShell process (PID 3876, ProcessGuid {47ab858c-e23d-5eac-c603-000000000400}) executed a script block named Get-PrivateKeys (loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) that enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and calls Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a thumbprint, writing each certificate AND its private key to a randomly-named .pfx in $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas'. The same process then created C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx and wrote certificate Blob values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\MY\Certificates\48B5E43D09D080DF8863152FD22ED7C43443D499 and ...\Remote Desktop\Certificates\615B93C2D2B647D1670500B3338EAAEC83BA5646. This is direct theft of authentication certificates/private keys (T1649). The parent process was a hidden, execution-policy-bypass PowerShell that decoded a bitmap-encoded payload (monkey.png) via IEX, indicating a compromised host.

findings.title: Outbound SMB/WebDAV to 192.168.0.4 and SMB to 10.0.1.6 from scranton (10.0.1.4)
findings.summary: Zeek conn records show host 10.0.1.4 (scranton) making repeated outbound SMB connections to 192.168.0.4 on ports 445 and 139 that were rejected (conn_state REJ, 0 bytes) immediately before the WebDAV HTTP traffic to the same 192.168.0.4 at 00:32:14-00:32:18, indicating the host was probing/being directed to an external SMB/WebDAV listener. The same host also performed large SMB transfers to 10.0.1.6 (up to 4,261,160 bytes) and SMB share access to \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\sysvol and IPC$ (10.0.0.4). The 192.168.0.4 SMB/WebDAV combination is consistent with forced-authentication infrastructure, though the SMB-to-10.0.1.6 and sysvol access are more typical of normal domain activity.

findings.title: accesschk.exe creates a 'passwordsDB' file on scranton host
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:04:35Z, Sysinternals accesschk.exe (PID 9204, running as SYSTEM) created the file C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB (Sysmon event 11). A PowerShell 4104 block at 03:04:34Z shows pbeesly invoking '& "C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\accesschk.exe"', immediately preceding the file creation. The filename 'passwordsDB' strongly suggests a credential-harvesting artifact written to disk, though the file content itself was not captured in the telemetry. This is consistent with collecting credentials into a file (T1552.001).

On scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe invoked csc.exe twice (02:58:45 and 03:08:03) to compile C# source into DLLs in random-named temp folders (qkbkqqbs.dll, 0piklvia.dll). This Add-Type style compilation is consistent with loading credential-access tooling in memory; the surrounding activity (accesschk passwordsDB, .pfx export, LSASS access) supports a credential-theft context.
findings.title: PowerShell compiles in-memory C# credential tooling via csc.exe on scranton

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe was spawned by powershell.exe under user pbeesly at 03:21:27. hostui.exe is a known UAC-bypass/credential-prompt abuse binary; an unusual parent (PowerShell) in this credential-theft context makes it suspicious.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, C:\Windows\System32\sdclt.exe was spawned by cmd.exe under user pbeesly at 02:58:42 (3 times). sdclt.exe is a known UAC-bypass binary; its invocation from cmd in this credential-theft context is suspicious.
findings.title: sdclt.exe spawned by cmd on scranton
SMB/WinRM/RPC traffic from spoofed 10.0.1.4 to NASHUA with Kerberos cifs/NASHUA tickets (possible SMB relay)
findings.summary: The spoofing MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 drives SMB (445), WinRM (5985), RPC (135) and HTTP (80) connections from 10.0.1.4 to 10.0.1.6 (NASHUA). Kerberos TGS requests for pbeesly/DMEVALS.LOCAL to cifs/NASHUA and HTTP/NASHUA are observed at 00:33:26 and 00:35:25, i.e. immediately after the MAC takeover begins. This is consistent with name-resolution/SMB-relay style credential capture, though no explicit relay tooling or LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning was observed in the PowerShell or DNS data.

findings.title: No credential-dumping tooling observed across process creations, script blocks or file writes
findings.summary: Stacking all 447 sysmon process creations and 460 security 4688 process creations shows only standard Windows/Azure tooling (svchost, conhost, powershell, cmd, rundll32, PsExec64/PSEXESVC, sdelete64, Azure agents). No mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, reg save, ntdsutil, vssadmin, diskshadow or drsuapi command lines exist in any dataset, and no PowerShell 4104 script block references lsass/mimikatz/sekurlsa/MiniDump/DCSync/ntds. The only .dmp files are WerFault.exe WER crash dumps. No evidence of OS credential dumping was found.

findings.title: LSASS handle opens with full access masks by PowerShell/wsmprovhost are .NET process-management calls, not memory dumping
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16, and PowerShell.exe (PID 3876) opened lsass.exe with 0x1000 at 03:01:03; on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29. The CallTrace for each shows managed .NET frames (System.ni.dll, Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll), i.e. PowerShell's process-management cmdlets querying process information, not a memory read/dump. No dump file was written (the only .dmp files are WerFault.exe WER crash dumps), and no process command line anywhere references lsass, comsvcs, MiniDump, procdump or mimikatz. The 0x1FFFFF opens by wininit.exe/csrss.exe at 03:19:09 coincide with a normal lsass process restart (PID 748, parent wininit.exe).

findings.title: SAM hive registry writes and SAM_DOMAIN/SAM_SERVER handle opens performed by lsass.exe (machine account) - normal OS activity
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, lsass.exe (PID 748, running as SCRANTON$) wrote HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F at 03:19:10 and opened SAM_SERVER/SAM_DOMAIN/SAM_ALIAS objects (AccessMask 0xf003f/0xf07df/0xf) at 03:19:11-03:20:46. These are the OS's own SAM operations by the Local Security Authority, not an external tool copying hives. No 'reg save', no SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive file copies were created (the only file-create hits matching SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM were Prefetch .pf files), and no process command line references reg save or SAM.

findings.title: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes by lsass.exe are normal cached-credential maintenance
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local lsass.exe (PID 728) set HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 four times between 03:11:40 and 03:15:03, and on scranton.dmevals.local lsass.exe set the same value at 03:20:46. These writes are performed by the Local Security Authority process itself as part of normal cached-domain-credential maintenance, not extraction of the cache. No process command line or PowerShell script block references cache, mscache or DCC2, and no tool read the SECURITY hive.

On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z, netsh.exe ran 'trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"' as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, and stopped it 7 seconds later with 'netsh trace stop'. Both netsh processes are direct children of the Microsoft Azure NetworkWatcherAgent service (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service), which was itself installed/started via its own enable.cmd at 03:20:41Z. This is the standard Azure Network Watcher packet-capture mechanism, not adversary sniffing: the capture is short-lived, writes to a GUID-named ETL under the agent's own temp folder, and is driven entirely by the signed Azure agent. No attacker-controlled process, no pcap output, no promiscuous-mode tooling.
findings.title: Azure Network Watcher agent performs a legitimate netsh packet capture on scranton

findings.summary: Across windows.sysmon, windows.security, windows.powershell and windows.other for the 2020-05-02 window, no sniffing tools or capture drivers were found: no tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap/dumpcap process creation, no Npcap/WinPcap/pcap driver image load, no pcap/sniff/promiscuous command lines, and no .pcap files written. findings.title: No MFA/smart-card interception artifacts; observed activity is PsExec lateral movement with cleartext credentials
findings.summary: Hunting for T1111 (Multi-Factor Authentication Interception) across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other and windows.powershell found no evidence of MFA interception. All credential-related hits are normal Windows components: CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service registration, Credential Manager (vaultsvc.dll), the Smart card PnP Class Filter Driver (scfilter.sys) MuiCache entry, RDP display driver (RdpIdd_IndirectDisplay) enumeration, and CredentialGuard being disabled (0x0) — all written by services.exe/System/lsass.exe on scranton.dmevals.local. LSASS access (Sysmon 10) is exclusively from svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION), i.e. benign handle queries, not credential dumping. The only notable credential activity is PsExec lateral movement: on scranton.dmevals.local, PsExec64.exe was repeatedly run with cleartext credentials (-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) targeting \\NASHUA to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, producing 4648 explicit-credential logons on nashua.dmevals.local via C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe and an RDP logon (LogonType 10, Negotiate) for pbeesly from 172.18.39.2. This is credential USE/lateral movement, not MFA interception, and no smart-card/OTP/MFA token artifacts exist anywhere in the data.

findings.title: Kerberos service-ticket requests (4769/4768) are routine domain authentication

findings.summary: No DHCP-related events exist in any dataset. The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP codes (1341/1342/1020/1063), the Zeek capture contains no dhcp log type (only conn/files/ssl/x509/dce_rpc/http/dns/kerberos/dpd/smb_files/weird/smb_mapping/notice/pe), and no DHCP-related PowerShell script blocks were found. DHCP spoofing is not observable in this data.

findings.title: No golden-ticket forging observed; krbtgt TGS requests are normal
findings.summary: The 4769 Kerberos service-ticket events include only one krbtgt request by pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL (from 10.0.1.4) and two by the SCRANTON$ machine account, all with Ticket Encryption Type 0x12 and Failure Code 0x0. All 28 4769 events use encryption type 0x12 (AES256) — no RC4 downgrade pattern, no anomalous krbtgt service-ticket volume, and no forged-ticket logon indicators. The 4672 special-privilege events (212) have no populated TargetUserName to stack. No golden-ticket activity is evident.

findings.title: No silver-ticket activity observed
findings.summary: The 4769 service-ticket requests are for machine accounts (NASHUA$, NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all successful with encryption type 0x12. There is no evidence of service tickets forged without KDC validation (silver-ticket behavior) — no anomalous service SPN requests or missing corresponding TGT requests in the zeek kerberos capture, which shows normal AS/TGS pairs.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting observed
findings.summary: No PowerShell script blocks referencing Kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/Rubeus were found (zero hits). The zeek kerberos capture shows only normal AS/TGS request pairs for pbeesly to cifs/host/ldap/HTTP services, with no burst of TGS requests to many distinct SPNs that would indicate Kerberoasting. The 4769 events show only 28 requests across a handful of machine-account services.

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting observed
findings.summary: The zeek kerberos capture shows AS requests to krbtgt that return KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED (preauthentication enforced) followed by successful AS exchanges — the normal preauth flow, not AS-REP roasting (which requires accounts with preauth disabled and would show successful AS-REP without the preauth-required error). No PowerShell script blocks referencing AS-REP/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth were found (zero hits).

findings.title: No forged web credential activity; observed activity is LSASS credential theft (T1003), not T1606
findings.summary: Across the Windows window (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) the only credential-related activity is credential theft from LSASS on scranton.dmevals.local by PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF and 0x1F3FFF, plus an obfuscated PowerShell script (ReflectiveDelegate/GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle + base64 shellcode) run as pbeesly. This is T1003 credential dumping, not T1606 forging of web credentials. No cookie or SAML token forging artifacts were found: the only cookie-path file event is a benign Windows INetCookies package file, and the Zeek window (2020-04-30, non-overlapping) contains only WebDAV file transfer (OfficeSupplies.7z, python.exe) with no web authentication traffic. The T1606 checks returned no evidence of forged web credentials.

findings.title: No forged web cookie activity observed
findings.summary: The only file event matching a cookie store is a single benign Windows INetCookies package file created by svchost.exe on scranton.dmevals.local (C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\...\INetCookies). No browser cookie theft, tampering, or forged-cookie authentication was observed. The Zeek HTTP traffic (2020-04-30, non-overlapping window) is WebDAV file transfer only, with no cookie-bearing web authentication. No evidence of T1606.001.

findings.title: No SAML token forging activity observed
findings.summary: No SAML token forging artifacts were found. No process command lines, PowerShell script blocks, or HTTP URLs referencing SAML/ADFS/token/assertion were observed in the Windows or Zeek datasets. The Zeek window (2020-04-30, non-overlapping with the Windows window) contains only WebDAV file transfer to 192.168.0.4 with no federated/web authentication traffic. The only anomalous authentication is a single NtLmSsp network logon (type 3) for pbeesly from 172.18.39.2 on scranton, which is consistent with lateral movement following credential theft rather than SAML token forgery.

findings.title: No MFA request generation activity; windows.other hits are benign RSOP/WMI operations
findings.summary: The T1621 hypothesis (adversary generating repeated MFA push requests to fatigue a user) is not supported by any retrieved event. windows.security contains zero 4625 failed-logon events, so there is no repeated authentication-attempt pattern. No PowerShell 4104 script block contains MFA/2FA/Authenticator/multifactor strings, no Sysmon process command line references mfa/authenticator/login, and no Zeek http/dns record references login/auth/mfa/okta/duo. The windows.other hits that triggered the check (event codes 5857/5858) are routine WMI/Group-Policy RSOP operations on newyork.dmevals.local performed by NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (ClientProcessId 1588), e.g. 'Start IWbemServices::DeleteInstance - Root\Rsop\Computer : RSOP_ExtensionStatus...' with ResultCode 0x80041002 — not authentication activity. The only credential-related activity observed is PsExec-based lateral movement by user pbeesly (LogonType 3/2, 4648 explicit credentials, PSEXESVC.exe) between scranton/nashua/newyork, which is lateral movement rather than MFA request generation.

findings.title: Routine Windows certificate store maintenance by lsass/svchost/taskhostw (benign)
findings.summary: The remaining SystemCertificates registry writes in the window are normal OS certificate-store maintenance: lsass.exe and svchost.exe updating AuthRoot and 'Windows Live ID Token Issuer' certificate Blobs on nashua/scranton, smss.exe creating the WOW6432Node SymbolicLinkValue, and taskhostw.exe writing per-user ACRS PhysicalStores values under the pbeesly SID. These are standard Windows processes touching trusted-root and per-user certificate stores, not attacker certificate theft. The WMI 5858 events are RSOP_ExtensionStatus DeleteInstance cleanup by SYSTEM, and the Kerberos 4768 TGT requests are ordinary logons for pbeesly and the SCRANTON$ machine account.

incidents.title: PowerShell opens LSASS with full-access rights on scranton (credential dumping access)
incidents.rationale: All six findings describe the same action: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff (PROCESS_VM_READ/PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, plus the wsmprovhost.exe LSASS access on nashua. This is the canonical LSASS memory access pattern for credential extraction, best fitting T1003.001 (LSASS Memory). F34/F37/F48 note the absence of authentication-process modification artifacts, so T1556/T1555.004 are not the best fit.

incidents.title: WebDAV forced authentication via davclnt DavSetCookie to 192.168.0.4
incidents.rationale: The WebClient service spawning rundll32 davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie pointed at attacker host 192.168.0.4 is the canonical forced-authentication mechanism causing the victim to authenticate and leak NTLM credentials, matching T1187.

incidents.title: accesschk.exe creates 'passwordsDB' file on scranton
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe accesschk.exe (invoked by pbeesly) writing a file named 'passwordsDB' to disk, indicating credential material collected into a file — unsecured credentials in files (T1552.001).

incidents.title: PsExec64 launched on NASHUA with hardcoded plaintext credentials
incidents.rationale: PsExec64 invoked with cleartext -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by on the command line is credential material embedded in a command line, matching unsecured credentials (T1552.001).

incidents.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports LocalMachine certificates with private keys to .pfx
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe the same Get-PrivateKeys script (readme.ps1) enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and calling Export-PfxCertificate to write private keys to .pfx files protected by hardcoded password 'saribas' — direct private-key theft, matching T1552.004.

incidents.title: PowerShell exports private-key .pfx to Downloads on scranton
incidents.rationale: powershell.exe writing coyn5igj.3io.pfx to the user's Downloads is credential material exported to disk; the finding is tagged as credentials from password stores (T1555.003).

incidents.title: SMB/WinRM/RPC traffic from spoofed 10.0.1.4 to NASHUA with Kerberos cifs/NASHUA tickets
incidents.rationale: Spoofed-source SMB/WinRM/RPC traffic to NASHUA with Kerberos TGS requests for cifs/NASHUA and HTTP/NASHUA immediately after MAC takeover is consistent with name-resolution poisoning/SMB relay credential capture, matching T1557.001.

incidents.title: ARP cache poisoning / AiTM positioning on 10.0.1.0/24
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 claiming IP 10.0.1.4 alongside the legitimate MAC, redirecting 10.0.1.4<->10.0.1.6 flows — the signature of ARP cache poisoning, matching T1557.002.

incidents.title: Outbound SMB/WebDAV probing to 192.168.0.4 and SMB to 10.0.1.6 from scranton
incidents.rationale: Rejected SMB connections to 192.168.0.4 and large SMB transfers to 10.0.1.6 are network connection/remote-service activity, not credential access.

incidents.title: PowerShell compiles in-memory C# credential tooling via csc.exe on scranton
incidents.rationale: csc.exe compiling C# source into DLLs in random temp folders is in-memory tooling compilation (execution), not credential access itself.

incidents.title: Invoke-Exfil script with hardcoded credentials and WebDAV exfiltration
incidents.rationale: The Invoke-Exfil script compresses the Downloads folder and copies it to a WebDAV share at 192.168.0.4; this is collection and exfiltration over web service, not credential access.

incidents.title: Steganographic PowerShell loader (monkey.png) executed hidden with execution-policy bypass
incidents.rationale: control.exe spawning PowerShell with -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden to decode and IEX a payload from monkey.png is execution/defense-evasion (PowerShell execution), not credential access itself.

incidents.title: Password-protected RAR archive created then wiped with sdelete on NASHUA
incidents.rationale: Rar.exe creating a password-protected archive of working.zip followed by sdelete64.exe secure deletion is local data staging and indicator removal, not credential access.

incidents.title: Suspicious .scr payload in C:\ProgramData\victim launched by explorer on scranton
incidents.rationale: The .scr binary launched by explorer.exe is the steganographic-payload staging binary — user execution of a malicious file, not credential access.

incidents.title: hostui.exe spawned by PowerShell on scranton
incidents.rationale: hostui.exe spawned by PowerShell is a known UAC-bypass binary invocation (privilege escalation/defense evasion), not credential access.

incidents.title: sdclt.exe spawned by cmd on scranton
incidents.rationale: sdclt.exe spawned by cmd.exe is a known UAC-bypass binary invocation (privilege escalation/defense evasion), not credential access.

incidents.title: python.exe executed on NASHUA via PsExec service under pbeesly
incidents.rationale: python.exe spawned by PSEXESVC.exe on NASHUA is remote execution via PsExec service (lateral movement), not credential access.
